svg.aria-label: Diagram: how an identity differs from a user account in Cloud Identity, the two ways the mapping between them can move underneath an existing IAM binding, why an unverified domain means the account behind a binding may not be yours, and how domain verification acts as a preventive control
svg.title: Cloud Identity: IAM binds to the identity, but everything lives in the user account
svg.text: An IAM binding names an identity. Everything that matters lives in the account.
The two are not the same thing, the mapping between them is mutable, and it can change without the policy changing.
Identity and user account are different things, and IAM references only the first
Thing
What it is
How it is referenced
Identity
An email address, and nothing more
user:alice@example.com
User account
The data, config, OU and group memberships
An ID not exposed externally
The policy can only name the left column. The right column is where the access actually lands.
Despite this indirection, any data and configuration details are associated with the user account.
Two ways the mapping moves underneath a binding you never edited
1. SWAP. An admin can change a primary email address, and can even swap those of two users.
The binding still reads alice@example.com. The account behind it is now Bob, with Bob data and config.
2. BALLOT. One identity can refer to two different user accounts — a conflicting account.
The user picks which account to use at sign-in. Your binding does not choose between them. They do.
And before the domain is verified, the account answering your binding may not be yours
A consumer account can be created with a corporate address. Its creator has full control of it.
You cannot control its lifecycle. You cannot enforce MFA. You cannot restrict the services it reaches.
A leaver keeps a trustworthy-looking address, and may convince colleagues to grant access again.
Domain verification is a preventive control, not paperwork
A TXT record proves you own the domain. It can take up to 72 hours to be recognized.
After verification, corporate addresses can no longer be used to create unmanaged accounts.
So the unverified window is where the problem is made. Verifying closes it and surfaces the rest.
The group in a binding is not a closed set either: groups can contain consumer accounts and members
from other organizations, unless you set disallow members outside your organization.
#31 called a principal a string. This is the post where the string turns out to have a joint in it.
OUs are not the answer: they look like folders, are unrelated to them, and are not for access.
